body: I requested them to not allow KCFI for userspace targets in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/105109#discussion_r1042552520. My understanding at the time was that you can't link KCFI compiled code against a libc which is not compiled with KCFI enabled. If I am misunderstanding this and this combination is fine, I don't have any objections against allowing KCFI for userspace targets.
author: bjorn3

body:
> I requested them to not allow KCFI for userspace targets in [#105109 (comment)](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/105109#discussion_r1042552520). My understanding at the time was that you can't link KCFI compiled code against a libc which is not compiled with KCFI enabled. If I am misunderstanding this and this combination is fine, I don't have any objections against allowing KCFI for userspace targets.

This is only true to the same extent that it's true for CFI - if you use a function pointer to a libc function, it will fail in both cases if the libc is not CFI/KCFI enabled.

Basically, the linkage is fine, and direct calls are fine, but if you do an indirect call to a `libc` function, that *will* fail.

It might be that when we stabilize CFI/KCFI in the future, we can partially address this by leaving kcfi as an unstable-only sanitizer on platforms where we don't expect the libc to be built with `kcfi` support. I think it's important to have something like this to ensure we can actually test both paths though.

@ChrisDenton, given that the immediate regression reported in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/122857 is being addressed by [the fix in Cargo](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/13630), I'd prefer if we fixed the rustc side via https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/115120, which already has [an MCP](https://github.com/rust-lang/compiler-team/issues/669) attached. It might take a bit longer to get https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/115120 merged, but I think even for this PR (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/123031), we'd need to do an FCP and I'd like to avoid the organizational churn. I'll push for https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/115120 being resolved asap.

What do you think?
author: michaelwoerister

body:
Sure. I'm ok with that. I do think the current behaviour of rustc itself is wrong but it's a long standing issue (cargo changes aside) so taking the time to do it right makes sense to me.

And personally I'll admit to always building with debug info so this isn't urgent for me.

body:
I pushed shiny new `rustc_layout` tests. There are two of them: `repr-c-int-dead-variants` tests `#[repr(C, u8)]` and is run for every platform and `repr-c-dead-variants` runs on four platforms: three major archs plus one ARM target that has interesting `c-enum-min-bits` (it’s done via `--target`, not `only-`, so it should be actually tested in CI).

I also added a line into `abi/compatibility.rs` that asserts the initial claim: `ReprCEnum<Void>` should be compatible with `ReprCEnum<MaybeUninit<Void>>`.

body:
It's 32 bytes large though, so using a reference could still save quite a bit of copying?

OTOH, `interpret`'s `Place` is 48 bytes and still `Copy`.
Do we have an accepted threshold for when to stop copying things around and start preferring references?
author: RalfJung
compiler-errors

body: most CPUs have a 64 byte cache line, so that might be a reasonable heuristic for when to *profile the difference*. trying to save on data copying when it is less than a single line often causes more thrashing because the result is that, especially in the big functions with complex loops that rustc can wind up having, you can wind up poking a bunch of different cache lines while trying to evaluate a function in a hot loop, whereas if you just copied all that data in you wouldn't have to worry about that as much.

body: I stumbled across this today while looking at `List`. I see `RawList` has been added without much explanation in the comments. It seems to allow an arbitrary header to be included before the list length. How/why is this a speed win in some cases? It seems very strange to augment a generic container type with an arbitrary value of a different type.
author: nnethercote

body:
There are some functions in the trait solver that use the [`TypeVisitableExt`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_middle/ty/trait.TypeVisitableExt.html) methods on a [`ParamEnv`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_middle/ty/struct.ParamEnv.html) to find out some property about the where clauses that are assumed to be true during trait solving.

For example here we disable caching here if the where clauses contain inference variables (which can happen due to [canonicalization](https://rust-lang.github.io/chalk/book/canonical_queries/canonicalization.html)).
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/5f8c17dcc04a2981268df89874203e9bfea50597/compiler/rustc_trait_selection/src/traits/select/mod.rs#L1508

Or here we find out whether inference has happened on the where clauses by resolving the inference variables. This has a [shortcut](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/5f8c17dcc04a2981268df89874203e9bfea50597/compiler/rustc_infer/src/infer/mod.rs#L1374-L1376) if there are no inference variables.
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/5f8c17dcc04a2981268df89874203e9bfea50597/compiler/rustc_trait_selection/src/traits/select/mod.rs#L574

---

Before this PR, the `ParamEnv` was represented roughly like this:
```text
               ------------------------------------------------------------
Clause         | type flags | outer binder | stable hash | predicate kind |
               ------------------------------------------------------------
               ^
               |
               +------------+
                            |
               -------------------------------------
List<Clause>   | length | clause 1 | clause 2 | ... 
               -------------------------------------
                    ^
                    |
                    |
               --------------------------
ParamEnv       | pointer   | reveal bit |
               --------------------------
```

So to find out the type flags or outer binder of the whole `ParamEnv` we'd have to iterate over all of the clauses. For some crates, in particular `diesel`, the `ParamEnv`s can get rather large (order of magnitude 100..1000) and iterating over them several times for every trait that we have to check adds up.

The main thing this PR does is add `ListWithCachedTypeInfo`, which stores the type flags and outer binder directly in front of the `List`, and use that new type in `ParamEnv`:
```text
               ------------------------------------------------------------
Clause         | type flags | outer binder | stable hash | predicate kind |
               ------------------------------------------------------------
               ^
               |
               +--------------------------------------------------------+
                                                                        |
                                 -----------------------------------------------------------------
ListWithCachedTypeInfo<Clause>   | type flags | outer binder | length | clause 1 | clause 2 | ... 
                                 -----------------------------------------------------------------
                                  ^
                                  |
                    +-------------+
                    |
               --------------------------
ParamEnv       | pointer   | reveal bit |
               --------------------------
```

This way, we can compute e.g. `param_env.has_infer()` in **O(1)** rather than **O(n)**.

`RawList` only exists to share code between `List<T>` (= `RawList<(), T>`) and `ListWithCachedTypeInfo<T>` (= `RawList<TypeInfo, T>`).
author: lukas-code

body:
Thanks for the explanation. In this bit:
```
                                 -----------------------------------------------------------------
ListWithCachedTypeInfo<Clause>   | type flags | outer binder | length | clause 1 | clause 2 | ... 
                                 -----------------------------------------------------------------
```
are the `type flags`/`outer binder` computed as a combination of the same-named fields from all the clauses?
author: nnethercote

body:
> are the `type flags`/`outer binder` computed as a combination of the same-named fields from all the clauses?

Exactly. The flags of the list is the bit-or of all the flags from the clauses and the outer binder of the list is the maximum of the outer binders of the clauses. 

They are computed when the `ListWithCachedTypeInfo<Clauses>` is constructed here:
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1189851eebdf6b69b164bbb7bf9df91188ae03aa/compiler/rustc_middle/src/ty/context.rs#L406-L412
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1189851eebdf6b69b164bbb7bf9df91188ae03aa/compiler/rustc_middle/src/ty/flags.rs#L38-L45

This allows such functions to become hooks (because hooks, like queries, print all their arguments via `instrument` ), which in turn allows me to eliminate more methods and state from the incremental-untracked CrateStore trait.

Unclear if we need that, but I felt like the closure API was weird and deserved a refactoring on its own

body:
As I we discussed on Zulip, I had two observations about this approach:

1. It doesn't seem to improve granularity if either one of the main or secondary type ids group them/put them all in the same group.
2. There will be multiple Reifying of types (which is what you're planning to do to solve the method to function pointer casting for KCFI anyway in #123052). Since we won't be doing this for CFI, I guess it'd require a secondary type id for all of these, which brings us back to the same broadness of checks that we've at #123082, but with diverging implementations for CFI and KCFI.

And as you noted:

It would improve:

1. Closures with captures would no longer be valid destinations at call sites that call function pointers.
2. Call sites that call concrete closures would only have the specific concrete closures as valid destinations, but these closures would still have the secondary type ids attached.

And as I noted:

1. Because these closures (2) would still have the secondary type ids attached, they would still be valid destinations at other unintended call sites.

We've come a far and long way away from the original [CfiShim](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/121962) [proposal](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/122573), which is great. If you understand the possible costs of these added levels of indirections for KCFI for cache coherence/locality and performance, possible introduction of gadgets or bypasses, and is willing to move forward with these on the Linux kernel (cc @ojeda), Android, and other embedded devices, I'm okay with moving forward with these changes. If this becomes an issue later, we can always revisit #123082, which works for both CFI and KCFI and doesn't require reifying types.

body:
`invoke` + KCFI operand bundles is [not supported](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/main/llvm/lib/CodeGen/SelectionDAG/SelectionDAGBuilder.cpp#L3307) in LLVM at the moment. All the other tests, even with the `-nopt` configuration, managed to avoid this.

An example of where this happens is that `core::ptr::drop_in_place<alloc::boxed::Box<dyn core::ops::function::
Fn<(&i32,)>+Output = &i32>>` will `invoke` its payload's `drop_in_place` method to ensure that even if the payload's `drop_in_place` panics, it still manages to free the memory in the unwind path. The KCFI bundle there errors out in LLVM.

After chatting with Sami (KCFI author), it looks like adding `invoke` support to LLVM wouldn't be too bad, but for now we might want to make KCFI require `panic=abort` to avoid `invoke`, since even if we fix it in LLVM today, Rust's LLVM won't have it unless we cherry-pick for a year, and LLVMs we support won't have it for two.

I'm going to set `-C panic=abort` on these tests to avoid this issue, and in a follow-up change will restrict KCFI to `-C panic=abort`. It may make sense to cherry pick a patch back to Rust's internal LLVM enabling `invoke` KCFI once it lands, and at that point re-allow `-C panic=unwind` + KCFI on unstable compilers with a rust-distritubed-llvm in order to keep unwinding KCFI tested.

body:
I was unaware that there is more than one variety of `ty::Coroutine`. There are in fact:
* General coroutines (which is what my solution works for right now)
* Async coroutines (what you've constructed)
* Generator coroutines
* Async generator coroutines

Since that value doesn't implement `std::ops::Coroutine`, generalization fails. I'm writing up a solution now that uses [`is_general_coroutine`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/nightly-rustc/rustc_middle/ty/struct.TyCtxt.html#method.is_general_coroutine) as an additional restriction on generalizing through `Coroutine`. Since async coroutines are supposed to directly implement `Future`, I'm generalizing them through `Future` instead.

See #123368 for an explicit solution to this issue, but it doesn't yet support generator coroutines or async generator coroutines, I'll find time to get those working soon.

body:
Not to bikeshed too much, but I think `separate` is an awfully non-descriptive name for what this method does. My intuition at seeing that name would be that it somehow breaks up an existing collection, not that it adds a new element between each instance.

Something along the lines of `interject`, `interleave`, `interweave`, `interlace`, or perhaps even just`separator` would seem more descriptive to me if the name just needs to be changed to avoid a conflict with itertools.

body:
`windows_sys.rs` is a generated file so any manual changes will be overwritten. See https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/library/std/src/sys/pal/windows/c/README.md

You can override definitions by putting them in `library/std/src/sys/pal/windows/c.rs` but ideally fixes should be done in [windows-bindgen](https://github.com/microsoft/windows-rs) (well, more likely the [win32metadata project](https://github.com/microsoft/win32metadata) from which bindings are derived).

body:
so the thing that is happening here is that previously, we set flags that say "disable this architectural feature", because we (and especially LLVM) allow target features to be disabled. this is a questionable choice to begin with, however, it's particularly problematic when considering that `-Ctarget-cpu`, which specifies a microarchitecture, comes with certain implied target features. disabling a feature takes priority over the implied features from `-Ctarget-cpu`, so most ways of specifying a specific CPU based on these architectures was effectively broken.

but we had to do something like this to make clear that the fpu was a slightly underpowered one relative to the full-bore Arm FPUs that they have nowadays. certainly not 32 128-bit registers! only about 16-by-32 or so? and this way fixes that by making only a positive statment.

the main question regarding this PR is whether this causes some oddity because someone was accidentally relying on us disabling those features. however, the new behavior will be more-correct in general, and we don't promise that our target feature settings for a given target remain static forever. and it's a fairly easy fix in general. in my experience, with dodgy feature settings that shouldn't work, it's far more likely they'll get a combination of effects that results in them failing instruction selection in LLVM, rather than emitting a bad binary that they can even try to run.
author: workingjubilee

body: That's my understanding of what's happening as well. This PR will result in the same set of features being enabled for users who do not use `-C target-cpu`. For users who do specify `-C target-cpu`, they will now get the features their CPU supports (according to LLVM), which could be a breaking change for a given project if their `target-cpu` is incorrect (or they have a version of that CPU that is under-spec'ed compared to LLVM's understanding of it, but didn't tell the build about this). Those users could add `-<feature>` to their build to get the old behavior (which is what they would have to do when using `clang` on such a CPU), otherwise they'll get builds that contain illegal instructions for their target. I'm not sure how this would manifest as ISel issues at build time though.
author: chrisnc

body: @chrisnc you know I had been thinking of any blatant contradictions (there are a few that toggling features on/off can get you, like especially with "use soft-float but use float registers") but I think those are less likely here yeah.
author: workingjubilee

But I'm having a hard time verifying that the new set of features is correct for the given targets, and I don't think we are actually executing any tests for these targets. @workingjubilee, feel free to r+ if you are confident in the changes. Otherwise I'll go look for another reviewer.
author: michaelwoerister

body:
The combo feature names this PR uses are defined here: https://github.com/rust-lang/llvm-project/blob/rustc/18.0-2024-02-13/llvm/lib/Target/ARM/ARM.td#L63-L91
(see `name#"d16sp"` and `name#"d16"`).

For `arm{eb,}v7r-none-eabihf`, the min feature set is of the [R4F, which LLVM gives `vfp3d16`](https://github.com/rust-lang/llvm-project/blob/rustc/18.0-2024-02-13/llvm/lib/Target/ARM/ARM.td#L1440).

For `thumbv7em-none-eabihf`, the min feature set is of the [M4, which LLVM gives `vfp4d16sp`](https://github.com/rust-lang/llvm-project/blob/rustc/18.0-2024-02-13/llvm/lib/Target/ARM/ARM.td#L1486).

For `thumbv8m.main-none-eabihf`, the min feature set is of the [M33, which LLVM gives `fp-armv8d16sp`](https://github.com/rust-lang/llvm-project/blob/rustc/18.0-2024-02-13/llvm/lib/Target/ARM/ARM.td#L1505).

For `armv8r-none-eabihf`, the min feature set is of the R52, which LLVM defines as ARMv8r and doesn't give a specific FP feature, but [ARMv8r implies `fp-armv8` and `neon`](https://github.com/rust-lang/llvm-project/blob/rustc/18.0-2024-02-13/llvm/lib/Target/ARM/ARM.td#L1169-L1170).
So this means the current feature list for armv8r is wrong and should be changed to just `""` to match LLVM. (Also, this change as-is will have the effect of enabling d32 and fp64 by default because they come with armv8r.) The manual is pretty clear on the existence of the SP-only no-neon version of R52 though. Maybe some Arm folks have other ideas about this? Is LLVM defaulting to a superset intentional?
author: chrisnc

body: I've removed the armv8r change as that requires more investigation due to how LLVM defines the architecture. The other changes should be good to go. I've confirmed that this allows e.g., `target-cpu=cortex-m55` to imply `mve`, and `target-cpu=cortex-r7` to imply `fp16` as expected.

body:
> However, it's also often equally easy to hardcode a size (e.g. `8` instead of `size_of::<u64>()`). Minimizing friction in the use of `size_of` helps  ensure that people use it and make code more self-documenting.

Could we then give a way that's less awkward?  People are still going to write `8` instead of `size_of::<u64>()` to avoid turbofishing.  Even `u64::BITS/8` is shorter and less symbol-heavy -- admittedly it also has a different type.

Can we just have `u64::BYTES`?  Kinda like how the problem with `std::mem::size_of::<T>() == 0` isn't the modules, but the fact that what I actually wanted was `T::IS_ZST`, like

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1c19595575968ea77c7f85e97c67d44d8c0f9a68/library/alloc/src/slice.rs#L846-L849

I've always thought that `size_of` being a special-cased function instead of an associated constant was a legacy wart.

(Of course, part of me thinks that [`usize` isn't even the right type for this to return](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1c19595575968ea77c7f85e97c67d44d8c0f9a68/library/alloc/src/raw_vec.rs#L36-L40)…)

---

Procedurally, BTW, why is this a PR?  Shouldn't it be an RFC, like https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/1030-prelude-additions.html and https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3114-prelude-2021.html were?  "[No new rationale](http://aturon.github.io/tech/2018/05/25/listening-part-1/)", and all.

The number of changes this PR is growing feels like the kind of high-impact change where the extra visibility and elaborated rationale of an RFC would be good.  For example, why not `align_of` too?  Hard-coding `8` instead of `align_of::<u64>()` feels like just as much of a problem -- maybe even a worse one, because at least `u64` is always 8 bytes, but it's not always 8-aligned.

Or is libs-api happy to have people propose prelude additions directly in PRs in future?
author: scottmcm

body:
> Can we just have u64::BYTES? 

Or `u64::SIZE`? `size_of` also doesn't say "bytes".
author: RalfJung

body:
> Could we then give a way that's less awkward?

I mean, I'd love to have a less awkward syntax than the turbofish in the *general* case, but we don't currently have one. I don't think there's a good special-case syntax for this, unless we wanted to provide a macro (e.g. `size_of!(T)`).

> Can we just have `u64::BYTES`?

I'd love to see that, but that doesn't help for other types, including user-defined types.

> For example, why not `align_of` too?

Zero objections, but I was trying to make a smaller change that would be less likely to have trouble getting approved.

> Procedurally, BTW, why is this a PR?

One way or another this needs rationale and an FCP. In this case, I put the rationale in the PR and commit message. I have no problem writing an RFC, but I don't know if the rationale needs substantial expansion or if we'd have consensus already with the current rationale.

Also, depending on the outcome of https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/121708 we may want this to be edition-specific after all. Either outcome would be fine with me.
author: joshtriplett

body:
> I'd love to see that, but that doesn't help for other types, including user-defined types

Could be an assoc const on `Sized`

I think that if this had been offered _before_ the `redundant_imports` lint, it would've been okay to use a more lightweight procedure.

With, I think we actually do need to sit down and wrack our brains for whether it's justified to make all -Dwarnings codebases rip this out everywhere.
author: workingjubilee

body:
> Could be an assoc const on `Sized`

Something trivial like `const SIZE: usize = core::mem::size_of::<Self>();`, I presume? My immediate thought is how this works given that `Sized` is a marker trait, which afaik requires the trait to contain nothing. Although I suppose it is already a lang item, so we could do whatever we wanted?
author: jhpratt

body:
> Something trivial like `const SIZE: usize = core::mem::size_of::<Self>();`, I presume? My immediate thought is how this works given that `Sized` is a marker trait, which afaik requires the trait to contain nothing.

I'm not sure about the exact rules, but the compiler does accept this addition right now. I think that restriction is about `auto trait`, while `Sized` is more deeply built-in (`#[rustc_deny_explicit_impl]`).
author: cuviper

body:
> Could be an assoc const on `Sized`

My concern with that is that it could easily conflict with associated constants on tons of other traits, I expect `SIZE` to be a relatively common associated constant name.

e.g. [this search](https://github.com/search?q=lang%3ARust+trait+%2F%5E%5B+%5Ct%5D%2Bconst+SIZE%3A%2F&type=code) has 1.9k results and I count several `SIZE` associated constants in common crates on just the first page.
author: programmerjake

body: Yeah, we had a lot of conflicts when `BITS` was added to the built-in numeric types.
author: saethlin

body: `const SIZE_OF` is much less common, but it's a bit Yoda-like to say `T::SIZE_OF`.
author: cuviper

body: I think it's going to end up being important to settle the question of the redundant imports lint before we decide on 1) whether to do this and 2) what approach to use to do this (e.g. edition vs everywhere).
author: joshtriplett

body:
We discussed this in today's @rust-lang/libs-api meeting.

Everyone was in favor of adding `align_of` in addition to `size_of`. (I've retitled accordingly, though I haven't updated the PR yet.)

We want to wait for the conclusion on the lint change before actually merging this. The amount of warnings that that lint change produces for adding a function to the prelude is very high, making it more difficult to introduce functions in the prelude.

The lint is very likely to impact libs-api policy on additions to the prelude. If the lint stays as-is, we're likely to only add items to the prelude in new editions. If the lint is adjusted somehow (e.g. by reverting it or by adding some kind of exception for preludes or re-exports), then we can add things to the common prelude for all editions.

Meanwhile, though, there seemed to be consensus to add these to the prelude, conditional on resolving the lint issue (and then deciding whether to use the 2024 prelude or the common prelude). So:

@rfcbot merge
@rfcbot concern settle-redundant-import-lint

body:
> > Could we then give a way that's less awkward?
> 
> I mean, I'd love to have a less awkward syntax than the turbofish in the _general_ case, but we don't currently have one. I don't think there's a good special-case syntax for this, unless we wanted to provide a macro (e.g. `size_of!(T)`).

Driveby comment: I really wouldn't mind having `size_of!` and `align_of!` that work for both types and expressions, and return an untyped integer literal. Having two different functions and needing turbofish for one is pretty awkward compared to other languages (C's `sizeof`/`_Alignof` and Zig's `@sizeOf`/`@alignOf` seem quite elegant by comparison).

Even if that doesn't happen, having something in the prelude here will be quite nice.
author: tgross35

body: @tgross35 How would that work? A type and value could have the same name, and the value isn't even necessarily of that type.
author: jhpratt

body:
> @tgross35 How would that work? A type and value could have the same name, and the value isn't even necessarily of that type.

that kind of thing is commonly used by [`syn::custom_keyword!`](https://docs.rs/syn/latest/syn/macro.custom_keyword.html), where it makes both a struct and a function with the same name.
author: programmerjake

body:
> @tgross35 How would that work? A type and value could have the same name, and the value isn't even necessarily of that type.

This could either follow latest definition, treating types as if they were defined at the beginning of their scope (getting a behavior more or less like C, ignoring forward declaration), or just always prefer the type. Not a concrete proposal so I am sure there are other holes...
author: tgross35

body:
That still wouldn't work, as `const`s and `static`s could share the name and be imported at the same time as a type. Don't get me wrong — I think it would be great. But I don't see how it _could_ work.

Anyway this is more of an aside to the PR, so let's take this to Zulip if you'd prefer?
author: jhpratt

body:
> Driveby comment: I really wouldn't mind having `size_of!` and `align_of!` that work for both types and expressions

Ironically we had `sizeof` and `alignof` (and even `offsetof`) reserved as keywords so they wouldn't even have needed to be macros, but those were undone in https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2421

body:
@BurntSushi I feel like the implicit criteria you're using for the prelude is different than the criteria I think we should be using.

Adding items (other than traits) to the prelude will never produce conflicts with existing code, since we allow shadowing. So, the main question I think we need to ask is "will anyone be confused if they see this item unqualified, without seeing anything introduce it first?". A particular flavor of that confusion is "will anyone be confused and think this is likely to be something local to the program or one of its dependencies?".

I also think the value of "seeing it introduced first" is limited, insofar as that *still* typically requires people to scroll up to the top of the module; *any* unqualified import should generally have a clear meaning to people reading, say, a modified line of code in a patch with just 3 lines of context on either side, without needing to look at the top of the module or get IDE assistance.

I think `size_of` very clearly meets that criteria. People aren't going to mistake it for anything else, and other crates are exceptionally unlikely to define a conflicting `size_of` that people are expected to use unqualified. Even unqualified, `size_of` has one clear obvious unambiguous meaning.

Beyond that, it doesn't need to be used in the *majority* of programs. Many items in the prelude aren't used in the *majority* of programs. I'd venture a guess that *most* programs don't use `Unpin`, or `ExactSizeIterator`. I would *bet* that more programs use `size_of` than use `ExactSizeIterator`. But there's still value in having all of those in the prelude.

On top of that, I think some people will feel as I do: "if `size_of` is no trouble at all to use, I'll write `size_of::<u64>()` instead of `8`". This is compounded by other languages having the equivalent operation built in.

body:
@joshtriplett Yeah I agree that `size_of` meets the criteria you outlined. But I feel like those criteria are coming at this from a "what are the downsides of something being in the prelude" versus where I'm coming from which is more like "I don't think `size_of` is used enough to deserve a spot in the prelude in the first place." A prelude forms a fundamental vocabulary, and increasing that has costs. It increases the surface area that is in scope in almost every Rust program. Each individual addition is arguably marginal, but if we don't stop to consider the overall effect of adding too much, we could easily wind up in a situation where our prelude becomes too big.

Like, I'm not totally opposed to this. I get it. I use `size_of` a lot and I get the reasoning that making it easier to use _might_ decrease the incidence of less robust code. I even agree that it might indeed do that. I'm just not sure it's worth the expansion of a prelude which really ought to be small. Every time we add to it, we use up a little more of our budget. Of course, we don't have any concrete notion of what our budget even is, which is what makes this sort of thing very hand wavy.
author: BurntSushi

body:
@BurntSushi
> what are the downsides of something being in the prelude

This *is* the angle I'm coming from, but I do want to take into account the criteria you're describing. It sounds like you're saying that items in the prelude have a weight in aggregate, such that even if one individual item meets all our other criteria, doubling the size of the prelude might be a cost in itself.

I'm not sure if I'd entirely agree with that criteria, insofar as I don't think that everyone needs to know about every item in the prelude. For instance, I think `ExactSizeIterator`, while self-explanatory in *semantic*, is probably something people would need to look up the exact definition of before using it, unless they'd worked with it before. Nonetheless, I don't think it does any *harm* to anyone to have it in the prelude; anyone not familiar with it will look it up, just as they would if it were an imported name. I think the *harm* it would do is if we polluted the namespace; for instance, we should never add a function `new` to the prelude because it'd be incredibly confusing.

That aside, though, even if we *did* agree upon that criteria, and agreed on the incremental cost of an addition to the prelude, I think `size_of` clears the bar for inclusion.

body: So what *shouldn't* be added to the prelude? Just traits and items with names that are a bit too ambiguous?
author: ChrisDenton

body:
> I'm not sure if I'd entirely agree with that criteria, insofar as I don't think that everyone needs to know about every item in the prelude. For instance, I think `ExactSizeIterator`, while self-explanatory in _semantic_, is probably something people would need to look up the exact definition of before using it, unless they'd worked with it before. Nonetheless, I don't think it does any _harm_ to anyone to have it in the prelude; anyone not familiar with it will look it up, just as they would if it were an imported name. I think the _harm_ it would do is if we polluted the namespace; for instance, we should never add a function `new` to the prelude because it'd be incredibly confusing.

Yeah I mean IDK if I would lobby hard to have `ExactSizeIterator` included in the prelude if we could go back and change things. Like, `Iterator` is clearly warranted but `ExactSizeIterator` isn't (IMO).

But yes, I do think that a large prelude---even if every item is unambiguous and not confusable---is a cost unto itself. It adds more implicit names into every namespace. Like, if I'm reading code and I come across something that I don't know, then yeah, I need to look it up. If I'm in my text editor, rust-analyzer can just take me to the definition. But if I'm reading code outside of my text editor (particularly during code review, but there are several other contexts in which this occurs too), then I usually need to resolve the symbol manually. The first step there is to go look at the imports at the top of the file. If the symbol isn't there, I usually get confused and start hunting around for glob imports.

I think that same sort of effect can happen with a `std` prelude that is "too large." It's not even about whether or not something like `ExactSizeIterator` (or whatever) needs to be looked up, but about where it is even coming from in the first place. If the prelude is reasonably small, then it's reasonable to expect most programmers to keep most of it in their head. And I don't mean a full understanding of every symbol, but just a recognition of, "oh yes, that comes from the prelude, I know how to look it up." A larger prelude, IMO, impacts this in a negative way. It's implicit context that is injected to almost every namespace in Rust.

The problem is that each individual addition is a marginal increase in cost. So in my view, adding something to the prelude isn't just about whether there are downsides limited to that specific addition, but whether its addition justifies that marginal use of our prelude budget in the first place. At least, that's my perspective.

Another way of looking at this is that `size_of` _may_ be deserving of a spot in the prelude, but I'm not convinced any of the rest are. Like I know `size_of` gets used a lot, but I don't think `size_of_val`, `align_of` or `align_of_val` get used even within the same order of magnitude frequency as `size_of` does. But it's hard to quantify precisely.

@Amanieu are you sure you got the right person or the right issue? I'm not -api


But since I'm looking at it I might as well comment. The feature is unstable and already requires `Hash` and `Ord` which may not be super-trivial so `Debug` doesn't seem too onerous on top. The only source of doubt I have is that I don't know which additional metadata types we might gain in the future (for custom DSTs? pointers wider than 2 usizes have been discussed somewhere...) and the fewer constraints we impose on those the better, maybe...

body: Sorry I should have clarified. I don't have any opinions on this, but I believe you did some work related to pointer metadata so you may have more context. If you're happy with this, you can just go ahead and merge it.

I'm working on niches for usize pointer metadata, which is only vaguely related since it doesn't affect the user-visible types. If you don't see any issues with API forward-compat then sure...

body:
We need an allocation to store the metadata for `ThinBox`. For ZSTs though, that metadata is always the same for a given type, so this PR makes it so that the allocation is created at compile-time and shared between all invocations of `ThinBox::new_unsize` with the same ZST type and unsized type.

The problem is that `ThinBox` stores the metadata immediately before the actual data. This makes it easy to dereference and get the metadata, but means that the layout of the backing storage cannot be described by a `struct`, no matter the `#[repr]` used. This PR therefore uses some hacks around `#[repr(C)]` and `MaybeUninit` to create a `static` with the required layout, but those hacks are really unclean (and in one case unsound, but that can be fixed). My question is whether `const_allocate` is useable enough to replace those hacks by a manual allocation of `'static` storage with the required layout, which would drastically simplify this PR and easily allow getting rid of the `Freeze` implementation.

body:
Keep in mind that in the future we may want to turn Freeze into a magic builtin compiler trait that allows no user-defined impls at all, and has a hard-coded set of impls provided by the compiler. The fact that it is implemented as a regular auto trait is a mere convenience, not something we want to commit to.

So, I think no API should be stabilized that relies on `impl Freeze`. At the very least that would require t-lang FCP.

I'm sorry to be the bearer of bad news, but you are breaking the implicit contract between compiler, language, and library here. If `impl Freeze` is the only way to do this then what you want is simply not possible with today's Rust, I am afraid. Just because rustc implementation details can be contorted into accepting code that does that anyway, doesn't mean this is something that we can just do. Keep in mind that the compiler exposes private APIs to the standard library and trusts that certain boundaries won't be overstepped. It would be a lot of work to enforce these boundaries technically so instead we rely on them being enforced socially.

body:
Sorry for being unclear yesterday, I feel like this led to some confusion. I'll start from the beginning:

`ThinBox` allows storing `?Sized` data in a `Box` while keeping the `ThinBox` itself a thin pointer. It accomplishes this by storing the pointer metadata in the same allocation as the value itself.

A naive version of that would allocate the backing storage like so:
```rust
#[repr(C)]
struct Storage<T: ?Sized> {
    metadata: <T as Pointee>::Metadata,
    value: T,
}
```
and keep a type-erased pointer to `Storage`. To dereference, it would `read` the metadata from this pointer and then reconstruct the full `*mut Storage<T>` from that.

This has the disadvantage of requiring (automatic) layout computations when accessing the value. To get around that, `ThinBox` employs a trick: the pointer points directly to the value, and the metadata is stored in front of the value like this:
```text
metadata | value
         ↑
      pointer
```
To read the metadata, we offset the pointer backwards by the size of the metadata, which is statically known. Then we can reconstruct the thick pointer from the metadata and the original pointer.

This PR wants to introduce an optimization for ZST values. For these, the only thing that needs to be stored is the pointer metadata, which is always the same for a given pair of `(T, Unsized)` and is `Freeze`[^1]. Therefore, this metadata can be kept in a `const` and can be referenced by all calls to `ThinBox::<Unsized>::new_unsize::<T>` for a given `(T, Unsized)` pair.

The problem we are encountering is how to construct that `const`. Because the pointer needs to be properly aligned for the ZST, the `const` needs to have the same alignment as the ZST. To keep this alignment, the pointer needs to point to the end of the `const`, meaning the metadata needs to be stored just before that. If the metadata has lower alignment than the ZST, this means there will be padding bytes *before* the metadata, like so
```text
| padding | metadata |
                     ↑
                  pointer
```
This kind of layout is sound, as the metadata is aligned, but incredibly hard to create using `struct`s or `union`s alone.

For instance, this PR currently does (simplified)
```rust
struct Storage<T, U> {
    metadata: <U as Pointee>::Metadata,
    align: [T; 0],
}

const STORAGE: MaybeUninit<Storage<T, U>> = unsafe {
    let mut storage = MaybeUninit::uninit();
    storage.as_mut_ptr().add(1).cast::<<U as Pointee>::Metadata>().write(/* metadata */);
    storage
}

let ptr = STORAGE.as_ptr().add(1).cast();
```
but if I understand #99604 correctly, this is not sound, as we potentially write the metadata into padding bytes, which are not guaranteed to be preserved when `storage` is written to the `const`. Also, to allow creating a reference to the `const`, `Storage<T, U>` needs to implement `Freeze`. This is sound, because the only thing stored in there is the metadata, which is `Freeze`, but because of the `[T; 0]` needed to provide the necessary alignment, this needs to be done manually.

To fix the padding issue, the `const` needs to be just a "bag of bytes" like `[MaybeUninit<u8>; required_size::<T, U>()]`. Because `T` and `U` are generic parameters, this requires `generic_const_exprs`, which is marked as incomplete.

The alternative, which avoids all those layout hacks, would be to use `const_allocate` to manually create the `const` and initialize it just like the non-ZST `new_unsize` constructor does.

[^1]: This is implied by `for<T: ?Sized> &T: Freeze`. #123206 will make this explicit.

What happens if there is padding between the header and the value? Then just subtracting the header size from the value pointer would give you the wrong offset, wouldn't it?

Oh I think I see what happens -- you compute the layout as if it as `(Header, Value)`, but actually *you don't use that header field*. body:
I think you are observing that what you want to do just cannot be done with current Rust, as const_allocation is needed, but that feature is far from ready.

I would recommend to restrict the optimization to types where the value alignment is no bigger than the header alignment. Then you can just create a promoted of type `&<U as Pointee>::Metadata`, and use a pointer to the *end* of that promoted as your value pointer.

body: Ah, new test.  I think issue #122805 is actually a good example of why this PR is overall good -- part of the problem in that issue was that this code was introducing `<2 x i8>` vector copies, which ended up confusing the optimizer into doing something unhelpful.  And thus this PR to stop emitting those vector optimizations will help avoid more impact like that.

body:
I've pushed a rearrangement of things to attempt to address the "tangled mess" concerns.

There's now a (non-exported) `ptr::internal_repr` module which is the only part allowed to know about the layout.  It exports two *safe* `pub(super)` (aka `pub(in crate::ptr)`) functions which are used elsewhere in the `ptr` module to implement the various `*from_raw_parts*` and `metadata` functions.

The resulting diffs outside the new module, such as
```diff
 pub const fn slice_from_raw_parts<T>(data: *const T, len: usize) -> *const [T] {
-    from_raw_parts(data.cast(), len)
+    internal_repr::from_raw_parts(data, len)
 }
```
seem entirely fine to me.

Like the previous iteration, there's no more need for `PtrRepr`.  Instead, there's just `PtrComponents` which is transmuted to/from.  And because it's only ever transmuted, the Copy/Clone impls are removed as unnecessary.

Personally I rather like it, since it lets stuff elsewhere in the library keep using the pointers they already have, rather than needing to cast them or wrap/unwrap them.  (For all that an extra `PtrToPtr` cast doesn't *really* matter, it's 1/20 of the default `#[inline]` budget.)

```
2024-03-31T16:20:49.6390268Z [TIMING] core::build_steps::tool::ToolBuild { compiler: Compiler { stage: 1, host: x86_64-pc-windows-msvc }, target: x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, tool: "cargo-miri", path: "src/tools/miri/cargo-miri", mode: ToolRustc, source_type: InTree, extra_features: [], allow_features: "" } -- 27.071

2024-03-31T16:20:49.7222796Z thread 'main' panicked at src\tools\miri\cargo-miri\src\phases.rs:93:10:
2024-03-31T16:20:49.7224192Z failed to determine underlying rustc version of Miri: CommandError { stdout: "", stderr: "" }
2024-03-31T16:20:49.7225165Z note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
2024-03-31T16:20:49.7271670Z Build completed unsuccessfully in 0:01:42
2024-03-31T16:20:49.7558528Z   local time: Sun, Mar 31, 2024  4:20:49 PM

2024-03-31T16:20:49.9281785Z ##[error]Process completed with exit code 1.
```
So, Miri failed, but stderr and stdout are empty. What? `CommandError` means the binary was successfully started, it just returned a non-success status code.

It doesn't even say which `x.py` failed. That's pretty much undebuggable... like, is this in checktools.sh or somewhere else entirely?

I'll try to get a bit more info out of CI. But that needs a bors run I think, as the x86_64-msvc-ext runner does not run in a PR? Or can that be changed easily?

@rustbot ping windows
if one of you could try running `./x.py test miri` with this PR to see what is going wrong, that would be very helpful. :)

body: Locally this (I tested `536afd3ae9e`) failed for me because `miri.exe` is failing to load `rustc_driver-*.dll` and `std-*.dll`. From the hashes in the filenames it looks like miri.exe in `stage1/bin` is trying to load the dynamic libraries in `stage2/bin`.
author: danielframpton
RalfJung

body:
The full order is [complex](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/dlls/dynamic-link-library-search-order) but for this scenario the two places I would expect to find it are either next to the `exe` or on the `PATH`.

Locally if I put the `stage2\bin` directory on my path then things end up running (although I see failures around actual output differed from expected due to local paths showing up in backtraces) but I am not sure that is the right fix here.

body:
Miri isn't really different from regular rustc here though, so it would be rather strange if it needed special treatment... How does bootstrap usually provide the right libraries?

I'm not sure if I'll be able to debug this by just throwing spaghetti at the CI runners until it sticks. This may need someone with a Windows machine to play around with the code.

We now have two invocations of cargo-miri shortly after each other: first to build the sysroot, then to run `cargo miri test` in the test-cargo-miri crate. I reverted the first invocation back to the old way (that I no longer want to use, if possible, as there's too many wrappers of nesting `cargo` inside each other), which is still working. The second invocation fails. This should be all the same binaries and very similar environment variables (and it seems like environment variables don't really matter anyway, except for PATH?), the only difference is
- The first invocation is executed via `cargo run --manifest-path=.../cargo-miri/Cargo.toml -- <arguments>`
- The second invocation directly calls the `cargo-miri` binary, instead of invoking it via `cargo run`.

Is `cargo run` doing some magic to make more libraries available to the program, like adding some folder to the PATH?

body:
Hm, I also found something interesting in the clippy code. Sadly with no comments explaining it. Instead of calling `add_rustc_lib_path` (which would be a NOP on Windows), they add some stuff to `helpers::dylib_path_var()`, which expands to PATH on Windows... But then they also immediately overwrite the PAH again with something else. I'm not sure if the clippy code works on Windows, but I'll try doing the "adding stuff to  `helpers::dylib_path_var()` part", maybe that helps.

I thought it would obviously be better to call `add_rustc_lib_path` instead of inlining it, but maybe its Windows behavior isn't actually helpful?

body:
The basic difference I can see between `rustc.exe` and `miri.exe` is that `rustc.exe` depends on the `std` and `rustc_driver` next to the binary, while `miri.exe` does not. By that I mean:

`build\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\stage1\bin\` contains (ignoring other things):
```
build\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\stage1\bin\cargo-miri.exe
build\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\stage1\bin\miri.exe
build\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\stage1\bin\rustc.exe
build\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\stage1\bin\rustc_driver-7c717ce3fea54cb2.dll
build\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\stage1\bin\std-16ca2320259178a1.dll
```
`build\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\stage2\bin\` contains (ignoring other things):
```
build\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\stage2\bin\rustc.exe
build\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\stage2\bin\rustc_driver-0c0d6e343a54bdfc.dll
build\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\stage2\bin\std-86a64ad04678906d.dll
```

The dependencies for `rustc.exe` point to the dlls in the same location:

`link /dump /dependents build\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\stage1\bin\rustc.exe` shows:
```
rustc_driver-7c717ce3fea54cb2.dll
std-16ca2320259178a1.dll
```

`link /dump /dependents build\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\stage2\bin\rustc.exe` shows:
```
rustc_driver-0c0d6e343a54bdfc.dll
std-86a64ad04678906d.dll
```

However, the dependencies for `miri.exe` in `stage1\bin` are the dlls in `stage2\bin`:

`link /dump /dependents build\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\stage1\bin\miri.exe` shows these deps:
```
rustc_driver-0c0d6e343a54bdfc.dll
std-86a64ad04678906d.dll
```

body:
> Oh, interesting. On Linux it's run from the tools-bin directory.

This may be a staging difference, not a platform difference. I do most of my testing with `x.py test miri --stage 1`, which then builds the stage 0 Miri and runs it to test a stage 1 sysroot. And we have this:

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/288daeb14f70192d53d2331b4c43a8c6d90d9d7e/src/bootstrap/src/core/build_steps/tool.rs#L822-L840

So for stages other than 0 we do some adjustment of the path returned for where to find the tool. That adjustment is strangely also tied to whether `add_bins_to_sysroot` is empty. And that adjustment *breaks* running the tool on Windows as it copies the binary to a location that has the libraries from the wrong stage.

@onur-ozkan you wrote that code in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/commit/6d99d6a9de9df76f47bccde605f5ec7f60bc2321. Is it possible that this copies clippy/miri to the wrong sysroot, i.e. not the one that has the libraries they need?

Specifically, `let bindir = $builder.sysroot($sel.compiler).join("bin"); ` is suspicious. That's the sysroot *of the compiler that was just used to build this tool*, which is one stage down from the programs that the tool will be used to run.

EDIT: I can confirm that indeed when I use `--stage 2`, it runs the Miri from `stage1/bin` with the libraries from `stage2`, same as on Windows. Except that on Linux this just works because `add_rustc_lib_path` actually does its job...

body: @rust-lang/wg-async Do you have any thoughts on this API?
author: Amanieu

body: How does this compare with an API like the one for `Error::provide`? I guess someone may want multiple extensions in the same future.
author: SkiFire13

body:
Yes, I think there will be a need for multiple extensions, but probably as traits and not just as concrete types, so I'm not sure if an API like `Error::provide` is quite right. Of course, `Any` is limited to concrete types so any traits have to be wrapped anyway. Maybe it could work. Each trait could be individually wrapped, and the consumer could request the wrapper type.

Another thing I believe will be desirable is overriding certain extensions in sub-contexts. For example, it may be useful to offer an extension for spawning tasks that could initially be provided by the top level executor but overridden to create task arenas. Maybe that could work with a provider-like API by chaining the provide calls up through the parent contexts, and the first to return something wins.

My main concern with a decision about this though is all experimentation would need to be against nightly. I would love to see the single `Any` field land in stable, and then in third party crates we create a provider-like API on top of that field and see if it sticks.
author: jkarneges

body:
> Yes, I think there will be a need for multiple extensions, but probably as traits and not just as concrete types, so I'm not sure if an API like `Error::provide` is quite right

With `Error::provide` you could just request/provide a reference of type `&(dyn Trait + 'static)`. 

> Maybe that could work with a provider-like API by chaining the provide calls up through the parent contexts, and the first to return something wins.

Yeah I think this could work nicely with a `Error::provide`-like API, you just need to have the child context extension store a reference to the parent extension and call `provide` on it if the child cannot satisfy the request. With the `dyn Any` approach you would have to store a raw pointer to the parent, which requires the user to use `unsafe`, and downcasting would no longer just work since you wouldn't get the parent extension.

> My main concern with a decision about this though is all experimentation would need to be against nightly. I would love to see the single `Any` field land in stable, and then in third party crates we create a provider-like API on top of that field and see if it sticks.

I'm not sure stable is the right place to do this kind of experimentation since if it turns out to be the wrong abstraction this is going to stick.

Also, writing a provider-like on top of it is going to require `unsafe` because ideally the provider would be able to store references, but `Any` forces it to be `'static`. You have the `Extensions` example for this, but I wonder if it's actually sound. What if you nest two calls to `poll` and get two different `'static` `Extensions`? Then you would be able to swap them, return from the innermost `poll` and still have access to its `Extensions`. This seems pretty tricky to get right.
author: SkiFire13

body:
> Yeah I think this could work nicely with a Error::provide-like API, you just need to have the child context extension store a reference to the parent extension and call provide on it if the child cannot satisfy the request

This is what I did here https://docs.rs/context-rs/latest/src/context_rs/waker.rs.html#9-12.

Two issues I see:
* this amount of indirection might be bad for wake performance.
* cannot provide through subtasks (eg tokio::spawn or FuturesUnordered)
author: conradludgate

body:
> I'm not sure stable is the right place to do this kind of experimentation since if it turns out to be the wrong abstraction this is going to stick.

By "stick" do you mean end up mostly unused? If `Any` has limits on what it can carry and thus experimentation with a known ideal data structure on stable might remain impossible even if the field were stabilized, then I agree that would be unfortunate.

I suppose it would be unfortunate not only for introducing a field that may go unused, but also because it would imply that experimentation with the ideal data structure would need to happen on nightly. That is a pretty rough fate.

If my example isn't sound, maybe someone else can come up with an approach that is. It's worth investigating very deeply into whether a simple field like `Any` can be made to work. Compared to the uphill battle of getting popular async runtimes to experiment against a complex API in nightly, it would be time well spent.
author: jkarneges

body:
Not objecting to experimenting with this, but registering that if this were up for stabilization I would currently expect to object to stabilizing it. I wanted to document this to make it clear that it's not as simple as "this solves the problem it set out to solve so let's stabilize it as-is".

Concretely:
- This is a lot of complexity to add to this interface.
- `dyn Any` is always painful.
- Sharing one pointer between multiple potential users is even more painful, and a Provider-style API would be even more complexity.
- Everyone would pay the cost of this, whether they use it or not. And to the best of my knowledge, this *isn't* something needed by all async runtimes.
- The potential users of this (AIUI) currently do have alternative solutions. Those solutions may not be *ideal*, but we have to weigh that against the complexity (which is a cost to everyone).

To be clear: still very much in favor of async interoperability, but I don't think this is a necessary component of async interoperability.

Request: please link to this comment as an unresolved question in the tracking issue for this.
author: joshtriplett

body:
> Everyone would pay the cost of this, whether they use it or not.

How so? It's just an optional pointer-sized field. If nothing opts-in to use it, then it's basically zero cost.

> The potential users of this (AIUI) currently do have alternative solutions.

Thread-local storage? Pass the data to the futures directly? These are not great options.

There's also waker hijacking via [waker_getters](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/96992). It's not stabilized yet and seems like a worse solution for carrying extra data than a `dyn Any` field (see conradludgate's comment), but I suppose it could be a better option than TLS and direct passing.
author: jkarneges

body:
We discussed this in the libs-api meeting. We're OK with merging this to enable experimentation on nightly, but nobody was very happy with the API itself. We should only stabilize this if we have extensively explored other API solutions (such as https://github.com/rust-lang/libs-team/issues/347, but that has its own drawbacks in terms of API complexity).

author: workingjubilee

body:
It doesn't just elide (), but also function items, and more (e.g., the extern function and the constructor that had to be wrapped in a reference in the tests so they aren't gone). For example, this made functions that had only one parameter that was a function item and otherwise were each one placed in its own group to be grouped together with all functions that were just `fn func()`, which was what happened with these examples in the tests. And this is just an example, any function that was disambiguated by a ZST had a similar grouping (or ungrouping).

But yes, we should wait the remaining patches to be merged and test this with them before merging. If we still find an issue, we should look into it and fix it, instead of work around it with this.

author: scottmcm

body:
> Maybe a silly question, but why is adding it here better than adding a bound to whatever wants it?

Adding a bound to whatever wants it would be a breaking change to add so we couldn't use it in e.g. std. Afaict we also expect all `Metadata` we ever want to be `Freeze` so adding it as an item bound doesn't hurt while making it easier to use.

body:
The PR description doesn't seem accurate to me. This impl existing or not doesn't by itself make things harder to optimize - the problem is rather that allocators are not bounded by : Copy and lack a way to get a ZST handle if that's possible for that type. This impl just makes it easier to accidentally pass an Allocator that's a ZST by reference instead of by copy which *does* make things needlessly slower.

I think the right solution is something like a `fn alloc_ref(&mut self) -> Self::Handle<'_>` on Allocator that lets you cheaply get a ZST handle...

author: estebank

body:
> This means that there will be some latent parent_hir_id calls that can potentially panic (on statics and RPTITs), right?

Yes, but that requires us to actually *call* `parent_hir_id` (or related fns) on RPITITs (in impls) and on these static allocation items (different than static items, which do have HIR).

If we find ICEs for those cases, we can feed their parent hir ids as well, but I would be surprised if we're getting HIR for either of these (especially the latter, static allocations, since those def ids are not reachable by anything except for metadata encoding).

body:
> tbvh, i'm totally lost now and dont know what to do next. this has been pending for so long

You could try:

```
$ git fetch --all --prune
```

or

```
$ git fetch origin master
```

to just update `origin/master`. You want to update your `origin/master` branch, otherwise simply rebasing onto your local master will still have the merge commits.

Then

```
$ get rebase origin/master --interactive --autosquash
```

To rebase onto `origin/master`, then drop the merge commits and squash your own commits into one.

Basically, I never use `git merge` or `git pull` without rebase.

body:
> As far as I can tell, CTFE, Miri, and Codegen all supported mixed unchecked shifts already without me doing anything. So this just gives a way to write tests exercising those.

This comment confusingly disappeared, but for CTFE/Miri it is true. The MIR binops support different types for LHS and RHS (and these intrinsics lower to MIR binops).
author: RalfJung

body:
> but it's the one that IMHO removes the most noise from the standard library code.

I was actually stuck on figuring the shifts out. Since you can have integer shifts with any integer rhs, backends will need to cast, no matter what, so I couldn't figure out how to make everything better for everyone.

I have all the other changes ready (I think), so I'll open a PR once we merge this (I'll try to review soon).

body:
It looks like the majority of the additional cost comes from additional indirection in calls to standard library functions, e.g., a diff like this:

```diff
-  f61064:       e8 73 f4 49 03          call   44004dc <_RINvNtCsavh3npScQaX_5alloc7raw_vec11finish_growNtNtB4_5alloc6GlobalECs1UKmS5rlRwk_21rustc_trait_selection>
+  ffe57a:       ff 15 a0 24 03 03       call   *0x30324a0(%rip)        # 4030a20 <_ZN5alloc7raw_vec11finish_grow17h78aea5cebcfaa28aE@Base>
```

This means more work, particularly for short-lived compilations, since the symbol needs to get resolved at runtime now. That cost should be eliminated with https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/122362, which might take some time to land but is making progress now. Most downstream programs also don't pay it since they're not linking std dynamically.

A little of the extra cost from there seems to be due to these non-inlined functions now being codegen'd with frame pointers (due to https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/122646). That doesn't seem like something worth worrying about, we accepted some regression from those changes already.

My sense is that something like this is probably still a good idea despite the regressions. We do see good improvements in binary sizes (including >1MB of librustc_driver.so), and bootstrap times are *significantly* reduced. That suggests that this is a pretty good win for the larger crates while being a slight loss for smaller crates (instruction count timings are down for some of the larger primary crates as well, e.g., ripgrep and cranelift). That seems consistent with the loss due to additional indirection due to librustc_driver dynamically linking with the standard library.

Going to mark as ready for review as such.

Test failures were real -- this change is making some inlining decisions change, and sometimes leaving functions that used to get removed entirely in the IR (since they're now `define ....` not `define internal`; we assume they might get re-used in a downstream crate's codegen, not that any of our codegen tests really have downstream codegen).

I made some adjustments to std and the tests themselves to reflect the changes. Not sure whether we want to move ahead given that impact, I think it continues to make sense to apply this change, but open to other perspectives.

Let's also gather a fresh perf run.

body: Do your local results show that the compile-time regressions will indeed be fixed by https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/122362?
author: lqd

body:
> Do your local results show that the compile-time regressions will indeed be fixed by #122362?

I've not checked against that PR. It's not clear whether our benchmarks are reflecting the full picture here: we see consistent, significant improvements in the rustc self-bootstrap times, for example. The binary size is also down (~1MB) which is also a win.
author: Mark-Simulacrum

body: Don't the 80 regressions on check builds indicate worse codegen on rustc?
author: lqd

body:
Yes, this PR is almost always going to be a regression in the direct results. Some functions that previously were inlined (or at least visible to LLVM) are now hidden, which likely regresses the call sites. But that is a tradeoff against the benefit that when doing that compilation, especially non-check compilation, we are able to avoid generating and re-optimizing a function that was already generated in some parent crate.

I suspect that in the case of rustc there are more(?) functions that benefit in comparison to the crates we see - most of which are library crates that are fairly self contained (i.e., likely aren't benefitting from reuse in a crate graph containing lots of instantiations of the same function).

I *think* the goal here is a good one, even if the road to getting there is bumpy. Ultimately to some extent if you annotate with inline(never) it feels semi-expected that we won't be inlining it.

I'll try to do some poking around to see if we should un-inline(never) some functions that are contributing most here...
author: Mark-Simulacrum

body:
Sampling a few cases:

* helloworld-check-Full -- essentially 100% of the regression is extra dynamic symbol lookup. This seems likely to be the "base" case, probably going to get mitigated by the static linking of libstd.
* serde-derive-1.0.136-check-Full -- regressions here are mostly due to alloc::raw_vec::finish_grow (+53 million instructions, 30/50 are in finish_grow and I suspect the remaining 20 are harder to track down but at least partially due to that function -- seems like there were a bunch of functions that probably got inline-shuffled due to calling finish_grow now vs. partially inlining it?)
* html5ever-check-Full -- finish_grow and dl-lookup
* ripgrep-check-Full -- finish_grow and dl-lookup

I think dl-lookup we aren't going to make any real dent in, though it might *look* better in the future with static linking and potentially with a newer glibc, which could optimize that more.

finish_grow was "the" initial thing which drove me to push on this thread -- right now that gets codegen'd in leaf crates, I suspect much of our binary size win on rustc is not having those local copies. Let's try without the inline(never) on it, see what impact that has. @bors try @rust-timer queue

body: Some sort of randomness with the begin_panic symbol, seemingly for the same builder sometimes showing `begin_panic::<&str>` and sometimes `begin_panic`. I'm pretty confused because AFAICT, they should have identical CI configurations. Maybe we're running into pre-existing instability/non-determinism with -Csymbol-mangling-version and -Zshare-generics?
author: Mark-Simulacrum

body:
OK, the issue is that if std is built with v0 mangling, then the test output differs. That only happens in PR CI today (due to https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/6b6a867ae9eac4e78d041ac4ee84be1072a48cf7/src/ci/github-actions/jobs.yml#L101), I started a Zulip thread about that difference.

For this PR I'll probably just normalize away the difference in the small number of affected tests.

body:
> The compiler (rustc 1.77.0) error for and_without_explicit_lifetime() in the erroneous code example suggests using a HRTB.

That's true but that particular suggestion is not super smart and has many issues (that are currently being worked on though) like #123713, #122714 or #122025. Therefore, it shouldn't be taken as a source of absolute truth.

For example, `rustc` currently suggests `for<'a> ... 'a` here:

```rs
fn and_without_explicit_lifetime<T>()
where
    T: Iterator<Item = &u32>,
{
}
```

which is not correct (#122025).

body:
This change looks like a strict improvement, so I'm going to approve the PR.

----

However, reading it raised a question for me.

According to my understanding of this PR, its effectively ensuring that `args` will be empty here:

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/9139d7252de74c30539afb35dc05e3536456971b/compiler/rustc_codegen_ssa/src/mir/mod.rs#L223-L224

which then implies that this loop will not have any `args` to iterate over:

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/9139d7252de74c30539afb35dc05e3536456971b/compiler/rustc_codegen_ssa/src/mir/mod.rs#L250-L256

What about the other components in that chained iterator, namely the `retptr` and the `vars_and_temps_iter` ? In particular, does processing the `retptr` ever imply that a function epilogue will be emitted (which should not be the case for `#[naked]`) ?
